items.stem: Two identical resistors of 24 Ω each are connected to a battery of 6 V. Calculate the ratio of the power consumed by the resulting combinations with (a) minimum resistance and (b) maximum resistance.
items.answer: Here R_max = 24 + 24 = 48 Ω (series) and R_min = (24 × 24)/(24 + 24) = 12 Ω (parallel). Since P = V²/R, the ratio of the power with minimum resistance to that with maximum resistance = (6²/12)/(6²/48) = 48/12 = 4 : 1.
items.ocr: MinerU spaced the digits, printing 24 Ω as '2 4 \Omega'; restored. The solution array garbled the final fraction; the ratio 48/12 = 4 : 1 is as printed.

items.stem: Let the resistance of an electrical device remain constant, while the potential difference across its two ends decreases to one fourth of its initial value. What change will occur in the current through it? State the law which helps us in solving the above stated question.
items.answer: According to Ohm's law, V = IR. Since the resistance is constant and the potential difference is decreased to one-fourth of its initial value, the current through the device also decreases to one-fourth of its initial value. Ohm's law states that at constant temperature the potential difference (V) across a conductor in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the electric current (I) flowing through it.

items.stem: Why are the heating elements of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
items.answer: The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, so an alloy produces much more heat for the same current. Alloys also do not oxidise (burn) readily at higher temperatures. Therefore the conductors of electric heating devices such as toasters and electric irons are made of an alloy rather than a pure metal.

items.stem: A V–I graph for a nichrome wire is given below. What do you infer from this graph? Draw a labelled circuit diagram to obtain such a graph.
items.answer: The graph is a straight line: as the current through the nichrome wire increases, the potential difference across it increases linearly. Hence V ∝ I and the wire follows Ohm's law. The circuit used consists of a battery, a plug key, a rheostat and an ammeter all in series with the nichrome wire, and a voltmeter connected in parallel across the wire.

items.stem: Why does the cord of an electric oven not glow while its heating element does?
items.answer: The resistance of the heating element of an electric oven is very high, so when current flows through it a large amount of heat is produced, it becomes too hot and glows red. The cord of the oven has a very low resistance, so very little heat is produced in it and it does not glow.

items.stem: Suppose your parents have constructed a two room house and you want that in the living room there should be a provision of one electric bulb, one electric fan, a refrigerator and a plug point for appliances of power up to 2 kilowatt. Draw a circuit diagram showing electric fuse and earthing as safety devices.
items.answer: The live, neutral and earth wires come from the mains through the main fuse and the meter. From them separate parallel branches, each with its own switch, feed the bulb, the fan, the refrigerator and the 15 A plug point for the 2 kW appliance. A fuse of suitable rating is inserted in the live wire of each branch, and the metallic bodies of the refrigerator and of the 2 kW socket are connected to the earth wire.
items.ocr: The figure printed here is the circuit diagram of the worked answer, so it is not attached to the question.

items.stem: The current flowing through a resistor connected in a circuit and the potential difference developed across its ends are as shown in the diagram by milliammeter and voltmeter readings respectively. (a) What are the least counts of these meters? (b) What is the resistance of the resistor?
items.answer: (a) The least count of the milliammeter is 10 mA and that of the voltmeter is 0.1 V. (b) Given V = 2.4 volt and I = 250 mA = 0.25 A, so R = V/I = 2.4/0.25 = 9.6 Ω.

items.stem: Write the importance of electricity in our everyday life.
items.answer: Electricity is used for: (a) Domestic purposes — lighting, heating and operating various electrical appliances such as a cooler, geyser, washing machine, T.V., etc. (b) Transportation — running electric trains, trams, etc. It also runs machines in factories, industries and food storage plants, and is used in shops, hospitals, hotels, offices and banks.

items.stem: What would you suggest to a student if while performing an experiment he finds that the pointer/needle of the ammeter and voltmeter do not coincide with the zero marks on the scales when the circuit is open? No extra ammeter/voltmeter is available in the laboratory.
items.answer: This is called the zero error of the scale of the ammeter or voltmeter. The zero error should first be noted and then subtracted from each reading taken when the circuit is closed; otherwise accurate readings will not be recorded.

items.stem: The current flowing through a resistor connected in an electrical circuit and the potential difference developed across its ends are shown in the given ammeter and voltmeter. Find the least count of the voltmeter and ammeter. What is the voltage and the current across the given resistor?
items.answer: Least count of the ammeter = 0.2/10 A = 0.02 A and least count of the voltmeter = 1/10 V = 0.1 V. The ammeter needle stands at 15 divisions, so the current = 15 × 0.02 A = 0.3 A. The voltmeter needle stands at 21 divisions, so the potential difference = 21 × 0.1 V = 2.1 V.

items.stem: (a) State Ohm's law. Write a mathematical expression for it. Or, state the law that relates current through a conductor and the potential difference between its ends and represent the law mathematically. (b) What kind of graph is obtained by plotting values of V and I? Why?
items.answer: (a) At a constant temperature the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends; this is Ohm's law. Mathematically V ∝ I, or V/I = constant = R, i.e. V = IR. (b) The V–I graph of a conductor is a straight line passing through the origin, because V ∝ I and therefore V/I is a constant.

items.stem: State Ohm's law. How can it be verified experimentally? Does it hold good under all conditions? Comment.
items.answer: At a constant temperature the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends; this is Ohm's law. To verify it, several pairs of readings of V and I are taken for the conductor and the V–I graph is plotted: it comes out to be a straight line passing through the origin, which verifies Ohm's law. No, it does not hold good under all conditions — it holds only at constant temperature.

items.stem: State the factors on which the heat produced in a current carrying conductor depends. Give one practical application of this effect.
items.answer: The heat produced in a current carrying conductor depends upon (a) the square of the current (I²), (b) the resistance of the conductor (R) and (c) the time for which the current flows (t), that is H = I²Rt. This heating effect is applied in electric heating appliances such as the electric iron.

items.stem: Give two reasons why the nichrome alloy is used for making the heating elements of electrical appliances.
items.answer: (i) Nichrome has a very high resistivity, so a heating element made of nichrome has a high resistance and produces a lot of heat on passing a current. (ii) Nichrome does not undergo oxidation (or burn) easily even at high temperature, so it can be kept red hot in air without burning or breaking.

items.stem: In a given ammeter, a student sees that the needle indicates 17 divisions in the ammeter while performing an experiment to verify Ohm's law. If the ammeter has 10 divisions between 0 and 0.5 A, then what is the value corresponding to 17 divisions?
items.answer: Least count of the ammeter = (0.5 − 0.0)/10 = 0.05 A. The needle stands at 17 divisions, so the current = 0.05 × 17 = 0.85 A.

items.stem: You have the following material: an ammeter (0–1 A), a voltmeter (0–3 V), a resistor of 20 Ω, a key, a rheostat, a battery of 3 V and seven connecting wires. Using this material draw a labelled circuit diagram to study the dependence of potential difference (V) across a resistor on the current (I) passing through it.
items.answer: The 3 V battery, the key, the rheostat, the ammeter (0–1 A) and the 20 Ω resistor are joined one after another in series, and the voltmeter (0–3 V) is connected in parallel across the 20 Ω resistor. The rheostat is used to vary the current; for every setting the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V are noted, and V/I is found to be constant.

items.stem: Calculate the number of electrons that would flow per second through the cross-section of a wire when 1 A current flows in it.
items.answer: Given I = 1 A and t = 1 s. Charge Q = I × t = 1 A × 1 s = 1 C. Number of electrons n = Q/e = 1 C/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 0.625 × 10¹⁹ = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

items.stem: How many 40 W, 220 V lamps can be safely connected to a 220 V, 5 A line? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Let x be the number of lamps, so the total power P = 40x with I = 5 A and V = 220 V. From P = VI, 40x = 220 × 5 = 1100, giving x = 27.5. Hence a maximum of 27 lamps can be safely connected.

items.stem: How much current will an electric iron draw from a 220 V source if the resistance of its element when hot is 55 ohms? Calculate the wattage of the electric iron when it operates on 220 volts.
items.answer: Given V = 220 V and R = 55 Ω. From V = IR, 220 = I × 55, so I = 4 A. The wattage P = VI = 220 × 4 = 880 W.

items.stem: 400 joules of heat is produced per second in a 16 Ω resistor. Find the potential difference across the resistor.
items.answer: Given H = 400 J, R = 16 Ω and t = 1 s. From H = I²Rt, 400 = I² × 16 × 1, so I² = 25 and I = 5 A. Then V = IR = 5 × 16 = 80 V.

items.stem: (i) Why are electric bulbs filled with chemically inactive nitrogen or argon? (ii) What is meant by the statement that the rating of a fuse in a circuit is 5 A?
items.answer: (i) To prolong the life of the filament; the chemically inactive gas keeps the hot tungsten filament from oxidising and evaporating quickly. (ii) It means that the maximum current that should flow in that circuit is 5 A; if the current exceeds this value the fuse will blow off and break the circuit.

items.stem: A current of 5 amperes is passed through a conductor of 12 ohms for 2 minutes. Calculate the amount of heat produced.
items.answer: H = I²Rt with I = 5 A, R = 12 Ω and t = 2 minutes = 120 s. H = (5)² × 12 × 120 = 25 × 12 × 120 = 36000 J = 3.6 × 10⁴ joule.
items.ocr: MinerU printed an intermediate line as '3600'; the product 25 × 12 × 120 is 36000 J, which matches the printed final value 3.6 × 10⁴ joule.

items.stem: V–I graph for the two wires A and B are shown in the figure. If we connect both the wires one by one to the same battery, which of the two will produce more heat per unit time? Give justification for your answer.
items.answer: The slope of the graph of wire A is more than that of wire B, so the resistance of wire A (R = V/I) is more than that of wire B. Since the heat produced H is directly proportional to R, more heat will be produced in wire A.
items.ocr: Reproduced exactly as printed. Note that for a common battery (same V) H = V²t/R would favour the smaller resistance; the book's solution argues H ∝ R and answers wire A.

items.stem: Can you run an electric geyser with power rating 2 kW, 220 V on a 5 A line? Give reason to justify your answer.
items.answer: Power P = VI, with P = 2 kW = 2000 W, so I = P/V = 2000/220 = 9.09 A. Since the line given is of 5 A, which is less than 9.09 A, the geyser should not be run on this line.

items.stem: In the circuit diagram shown, the two resistance wires A and B are of the same length and same material, but A is thicker than B. Which ammeter, A₁ or A₂, will indicate the higher reading for current? Give reason.
items.answer: Ammeter A₁ will show the higher reading. Because wire A is thicker than wire B it has a larger area of cross-section and hence a smaller resistance, so the current drawn through A from the battery is more, and the ammeter A₁ in its branch shows the higher reading.

items.stem: Give reasons for the following: (i) What do you understand by the term fuse in an electric circuit? (ii) Fuse wire is placed in series with the device.
items.answer: (i) A fuse is the weakest link placed in series in an electric circuit, which melts when the circuit gets overloaded or short circuited. (ii) Being in series, the whole current of the circuit passes through the fuse, so it melts and stops the flow of any unduly high electric current, breaking the circuit and protecting the device.

items.stem: An electric lamp is marked 220 V, 100 W. It is used for 5 hours daily. Calculate: (a) its resistance while glowing, (b) energy consumed in kWh/day.
items.answer: (a) P = 100 W and V = 220 V, so the resistance while glowing R = V²/P = (220 × 220)/100 = 484 Ω. (b) t = 5 hours daily, so the energy consumed per day E = P·t = 100 W × 5 h = 500 Wh = 500/1000 kWh = 0.5 kWh.

items.stem: 40 joules of work is done in moving a charge from a point at 230 volts to another point at 240 volts. Find the quantity of the charge.
items.answer: Potential difference V = 240 − 230 = 10 volts and work done W = 40 J. Since V = W/Q, Q = W/V = 40/10 = 4 coulomb.

items.stem: The filament of an electric lamp draws a current of 0.5 amperes, which lights for 4 hours. Calculate the amount of charge that flows through the circuit.
items.answer: Current I = 0.5 A and time t = 4 hours = 4 × 60 × 60 = 14400 s. Charge Q = I × t = 0.5 × 14400 = 7200 coulomb.

items.stem: Calculate the current in the wire if a charge of 1800 coulombs flows through it in 3 minutes.
items.answer: Charge Q = 1800 coulomb and time t = 3 minutes = 3 × 60 = 180 s. Current I = Q/t = 1800/180 = 10 A.

items.stem: 10²¹ electrons, each having a charge of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, pass from a point P towards another point Q in 0.1 s. What is the current? What is the direction of the conventional current?
items.answer: (i) Total charge = number of electrons × charge on one electron = 10²¹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 160 C. With t = 0.1 s, I = Q/t = 160/0.1 = 1600 A. (ii) Electrons travel from P to Q, so the direction of the conventional current is from Q to P.

items.stem: A TV set shoots out a beam of electrons. The beam current is 10 µA. How many electrons strike the TV screen in each second? How much charge strikes the screen in a minute?
items.answer: Given I = 10 µA = 10 × 10⁻⁶ A. For t = 1 second, the number of electrons n = It/e = (10 × 10⁻⁶ × 1)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹³ electrons. In one minute the charge Q = It = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 60 = 600 × 10⁻⁶ C = 600 µC.

items.stem: What is the potential difference between the terminals of a battery if 250 joules of work is required to transfer 25 coulombs of charge from one terminal of the battery to the other?
items.answer: Work done W = 250 joules and charge Q = 25 coulombs. Potential difference V = W/Q = 250/25 = 10 volts.

items.stem: A resistance of 0.05 ohm has a current of 3 amperes flowing in it. Calculate the potential difference across its ends.
items.answer: Resistance R = 0.05 Ω and current I = 3 A. Since R = V/I, V = R × I = 0.05 × 3 = 0.15 volt.

items.stem: How does the resistance of a wire affect the flow of current?
items.answer: The flow of current is due to the flow of electrons, but the electrons in a conductor cannot move freely because of the attraction of the atoms among which they move. This results in retardation of the flow of electrons; in other words, the resistance of the conductor opposes and reduces the flow of current.

items.stem: (a) What material is used in making the filament of an electric bulb? (b) Name the characteristics which make it suitable for this.
items.answer: (a) Tungsten is used in making the filament of an electric bulb. (b) Tungsten has a very high melting point, so it can be kept white hot without melting, and it has a high resistivity, so it retains much heat and glows brightly.

items.stem: In an electric circuit with a resistance wire and a cell, the current flowing is I. What would happen to this current if the wire is replaced by another thicker wire of the same material and same length? Give reason.
items.answer: The current flowing through the thicker wire increases. When the wire is replaced by a thicker one its area of cross-section is larger, so from R = ρl/A its resistance decreases, and consequently the current I = V/R increases.

items.stem: The resistance of a metal wire of length 2 metres and area of cross-section 1.55 × 10⁻⁶ m² is 0.036 Ω. Calculate the resistivity of the metal.

What is electrical resistivity? In a series electrical circuit comprising a resistor made up of a metallic wire, the ammeter reads 5 A. The reading of the ammeter decreases to half when the length of the wire is doubled. Why?
items.answer: The electrical resistivity of a material is the resistance offered to the flow of current by a conductor of that material of unit length and unit area of cross-section. If the length of the wire is doubled, l' = 2l, and since R = ρl/A the resistance is doubled. As I = V/R, the new current I' = VA/(ρl') = ½ × VA/(ρl) = I/2, so the ammeter reading falls to half, from 5 A to 2.5 A.

items.stem: An aluminium wire has a radius of 0.25 mm and a length of 75 m. If the resistance of the wire is 10 Ω, calculate the resistivity of aluminium.
items.answer: From R = ρl/A = ρl/(πr²), the resistivity ρ = Rπr²/l = [10 × 3.14 × (0.25 × 10⁻³)²]/75 = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.

items.stem: Distinguish between the terms overloading and short-circuiting as used in domestic circuits.
items.answer: (i) Short-circuiting occurs when a live wire comes in contact with a neutral wire, whereas overloading occurs when many electrical appliances of high power ratings are operated at the same time. (ii) In short-circuiting a very large current flows through the circuit because the resistance of the path formed where the two wires touch is very small; in overloading a large current is drawn from the electric supply because of the simultaneous use of many appliances.

items.stem: A piece of wire of resistance 20 Ω is drawn out so that its length is increased to twice its original length. Calculate the resistance of the wire in the new situation.
items.answer: Let the original length be l, so R₀ = ρl/A = 20 Ω. The new length l' = 2l and, as the volume of the wire stays constant, Al = A'l' gives A' = A/2. The new resistance Rₙ = ρl'/A' = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4(ρl/A) = 4R₀ = 4 × 20 = 80 Ω.

items.stem: A copper wire has a diameter of 0.5 mm and a resistivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ ohm-cm. How much of this wire would be necessary to make a resistance of 10 ohm?
items.answer: Radius of the wire r = d/2 = 0.5/2 = 0.25 mm = 0.025 cm. Since R = ρl/A, the length l = RA/ρ = Rπr²/ρ = 10 × (22/7) × (0.025)²/(1.6 × 10⁻⁶) = 122.67 cm.

items.stem: A copper wire of length 3 m and area of cross-section 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ m² has a resistance of 3 × 10⁻² ohms. Calculate the resistivity of copper.
items.answer: Given l = 3 m, A = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ m² and R = 3 × 10⁻² Ω. From R = ρl/A, ρ = RA/l = (3 × 10⁻² × 1.7 × 10⁻⁶)/3 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by electric resistance of a conductor? (b) A wire of length L and resistance R is stretched so that the length is doubled and the area of cross section is halved. How will (i) resistance change and (ii) resistivity change?
items.answer: (a) The resistance of a conductor means the obstruction it offers to the flow of current through it. (b) The new length L' = 2L and the new area A' = A/2. (i) R' = ρL'/A' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4ρL/A = 4R, so the resistance becomes four times. (ii) Resistivity depends only on the material of the wire, so the resistivity remains the same.

items.stem: How do currents in different resistors vary if they are connected in parallel?
items.answer: In a parallel combination the same potential difference acts across every resistor, so the currents in the different resistors are inversely proportional to their resistances: the higher the resistance of a branch, the less is the current through it. The total current is the sum of the currents flowing in the different branches.

items.stem: If five resistances each of value 0.5 ohm are connected in series, what will be the resultant resistance?
items.answer: Resultant resistance R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + R₄ + R₅ = (0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5) Ω = 2.5 Ω.

items.stem: Suppose a 6 volt battery is connected across a lamp whose resistance is 20 ohm through a variable resistor as shown in the given figure. If the current in the circuit is 0.25 A, find out the resistance of the variable resistor.
items.answer: Let R₁ be the resistance required from the variable resistor, so the total resistance in the circuit R = 20 Ω + R₁. By Ohm's law I = V/R, so 0.25 A = 6 V/(20 Ω + R₁), giving 20 + R₁ = 6/0.25 = 24 and R₁ = 4 ohm.

items.stem: How are three resistors joined in parallel? What is the potential difference across each resistor joined in parallel?
items.answer: (a) Three resistors are said to be joined in parallel when one end of all the three resistors is joined to one terminal of the battery and the other end of all three is joined to the other terminal of the battery. (b) The potential difference between the junction points A and B is the same across each resistor and equals the voltage of the battery.

items.stem: In the given circuit diagram suppose the resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ have the values 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 30 Ω respectively, which have been connected to a battery of 12 volt. Calculate (a) the current through each resistor, (b) the total current in the circuit and (c) the total circuit resistance.
items.answer: The resistors are in parallel, so the 12 V of the battery acts across each of them. (a) I₁ = V/R₁ = 12/5 = 2.4 A, I₂ = 12/10 = 1.2 A and I₃ = 12/30 = 0.4 A. (b) Total current I = 2.4 + 1.2 + 0.4 = 4 A. (c) 1/R = 1/5 + 1/10 + 1/30 = 1/3, so the total resistance R = 3 Ω.

items.stem: Three 2 Ω resistors A, B and C are connected as shown in the figure. Each of them dissipates energy and can withstand a maximum power of 18 W without melting. Find the maximum current that can flow through the three resistors.
items.answer: For resistor A, the maximum current I = √(P/R) = √(18/2) = 3 A. Resistors B and C are connected in parallel with each other and have equal resistance, so the current through A divides equally between them: the maximum current through each of B and C is 3 × ½ = 1.5 A.

items.stem: Is it possible to connect the different resistors in both combinations (i.e. series and parallel) together? Draw a diagram to illustrate it.
items.answer: Yes, it is possible to have resistors in both combinations together, that is in a mixed (series–parallel) combination. For example, two resistors may be joined in parallel with each other and this parallel combination joined in series with a third resistor and the cell.

items.stem: Draw a schematic diagram of a circuit consisting of a 24 V battery, a 10 ohm resistor, a 5 ohm resistor, a 1 ohm resistor, an ammeter and a plug key, all connected in series. Calculate the ammeter reading in this circuit.
items.answer: All the resistances are connected in series, so the equivalent resistance R = 10 + 5 + 1 = 16 Ω with V = 24 volt. The current I = V/R = 24/16 = 1.5 A, so the ammeter reading is 1.5 A.
items.ocr: The schematic is drawn in the worked answer, so no figure is attached. The calculation of the ammeter reading resumes at the top of page 32; the halves were joined.

items.stem: A wire is cut into three equal parts and then connected in parallel. How will its (a) resistance and (b) resistivity get affected?
items.answer: (a) Let the resistance of the whole wire be R Ω. When it is cut into three equal parts, each part has resistance R/3. Connecting these in parallel, 1/Rp = 3/(R/3) = 9/R, so Rp = R/9 — the resistance becomes one-ninth of the original. (b) Resistivity depends only on the material of the wire, so it remains the same.

items.stem: Calculate the current flowing through the resistors.
items.answer: In the given circuit the resistors R₁ = 2 Ω and R₂ = 4 Ω are connected in parallel, so 1/R = 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4 and R = 4/3 Ω. With the 4 V supply, the current I = V/R = 4/(4/3) = 3 A.

items.stem: (a) What is the total resistance of n resistors each of resistance R connected in (i) series, (ii) parallel? (b) Calculate the resultant resistance of 3 resistors 3 Ω, 4 Ω and 12 Ω connected in parallel.
items.answer: (a) (i) In series, Rs = R + R + R + ... up to n times = nR. (ii) In parallel, 1/Rp = 1/R + 1/R + ... up to n times = n/R, so Rp = R/n. (b) 1/Rp = 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/12 = (4 + 3 + 1)/12 = 8/12, so Rp = 12/8 = 1.5 Ω.

items.stem: In the above circuit diagram calculate (a) the value of current through each resistor, (b) the total current in the circuit and (c) the total effective resistance of the circuit.
items.answer: Here R₁ = 5 Ω, R₂ = 10 Ω and R₃ = 30 Ω are in parallel across V = 6 volt. (a) I₁ = V/R₁ = 6/5 = 1.2 A, I₂ = 6/10 = 0.6 A and I₃ = 6/30 = 0.2 A. (b) Total current I = 1.2 + 0.6 + 0.2 = 2 A. (c) 1/Rp = 1/5 + 1/10 + 1/30 = (6 + 3 + 1)/30 = 10/30 = 1/3, so Rp = 3 Ω.

items.stem: Two resistors of resistances 3 Ω and 6 Ω respectively are connected to a battery of 6 V so as to have (a) maximum resistance, (b) maximum current. (i) How will you connect the resistances in each case? (ii) Calculate the strength of the current in the circuit in both cases.
items.answer: (a) For maximum resistance the resistors are connected in series: Rs = R₁ + R₂ = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω, so the current Is = V/Rs = 6/9 = 0.67 A. (b) For maximum current the resistance must be minimum, so the resistors are connected in parallel: 1/Rp = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, giving Rp = 2 Ω and Ip = V/Rp = 6/2 = 3 A.

items.stem: What would be the readings of the ammeter and voltmeter in the given circuit?
items.answer: In the given circuit all the resistors are connected in series, so the equivalent resistance R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 Ω. The voltage V = 3 volt, so I = V/R = 3/6 = 0.5 A and the reading of the ammeter will be 0.5 A. The voltmeter, connected across the 1 Ω resistor, reads V = IR = 0.5 × 1 = 0.5 V.

items.stem: Calculate the effective resistance between P and Q.
items.answer: The three resistors lie in parallel between P and Q, so 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ = 1/1 + 1/10 + 1/10 = (10 + 1 + 1)/10 = 12/10 = 6/5, giving the effective resistance R = 5/6 Ω.

items.stem: How would the reading of the voltmeter change if it is connected between B and C?
items.answer: In the given circuit R₁ = 1 Ω, R₂ = 2 Ω and R₃ = 3 Ω are connected in series, so R = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 Ω. With V = 3 volt, I = V/R = 3/6 = ½ A. Across the 1 Ω resistor the voltmeter reads V₁ = IR = ½ × 1 = 0.5 V, whereas between B and C, across the 3 Ω resistor, it would read V₂ = ½ × 3 = 1.5 V. So the reading increases from 0.5 V to 1.5 V.

items.stem: An electric heater connected to a 220 V line has two resistance coils of 22 ohms each. Calculate the current if these coils are used (a) separately, (b) in series, (c) in parallel.
items.answer: (a) Separately: I = V/R = 220/22 = 10 A. (b) In series: R = R₁ + R₂ = 22 + 22 = 44 Ω, so I = V/R = 220/44 = 5 A. (c) In parallel: 1/R = 1/22 + 1/22 = 1/11, so R = 11 Ω and I = V/R = 220/11 = 20 A.

items.stem: Calculate the equivalent resistance from the following combination of resistors.
items.answer: In the given circuit the 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors are connected in series, so Rs = R₁ + R₂ = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω. For the parallel section, 1/Rp = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1, so Rp = 1 Ω.

items.stem: If in figure A, R₁ = 10 Ω, R₂ = 40 Ω, R₃ = 30 Ω, R₄ = 20 Ω, R₅ = 60 Ω and a 12 V battery are connected to the arrangement, calculate (a) total resistance in the circuit and (b) total current flowing in the circuit.
items.answer: For the first parallel group, 1/RA = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/10 + 1/40 = 5/40, so RA = 8 Ω. For the second group, 1/RB = 1/R₃ + 1/R₄ + 1/R₅ = 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/60 = 6/60, so RB = 10 Ω. (a) The two groups are in series, so the total resistance R = RA + RB = 8 + 10 = 18 Ω. (b) Total current I = V/R = 12/18 = 2/3 A ≈ 0.67 A.

items.stem: Write the applications of the heating effect of current.
items.answer: (a) The heating effect of current is utilised in many electrical appliances such as the room heater, electric iron, electric toaster and electric lamp. (b) It is also used in the electric fuse, which melts and breaks the circuit when too large a current flows.

items.stem: How much work is done during the flow of current for a given time in a wire?
items.answer: Since a conductor offers resistance to the flow of current, work has to be done continuously to move the electrons and maintain the current. The work done in carrying a charge Q through a potential difference V is W = Q × V. As Q = I × t, W = V × I × t, and by Ohm's law V = IR, so W = I²Rt. Since energy is the capacity to do work, the electrical energy converted is H = I²Rt.

items.stem: Express Joule's law of heating mathematically. What is the resistance of a 12 m wire having radius 2 × 10⁻⁴ m and specific resistivity 3.14 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m?
items.answer: In accordance with Joule's law of heating, if a current I flows through a resistor of resistance R for a time t, the heat produced across the resistor is H = I²Rt joules. For the given wire, R = ρl/A = ρl/(πr²) = (12 × 3.14 × 10⁻⁸)/(3.14 × 4 × 10⁻⁸) = 3 Ω.

items.stem: Study the following circuit and answer the following questions: (a) State the type of combination of the two resistors in the circuit. (b) How much current is flowing through (i) the 10 Ω and (ii) the 15 Ω resistors? (c) What is the ammeter reading?
items.answer: (a) Parallel combination. (b) With 3 V across each resistor, I₁ = V/R₁ = 3/10 = 0.3 A through the 10 Ω resistor and I₂ = V/R₂ = 3/15 = 0.2 A through the 15 Ω resistor. (c) The current flowing in the circuit is I₁ + I₂ = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 A, so the ammeter reading will be 0.5 A.

items.stem: Calculate the electrical energy consumed by a 1200 W toaster in 20 minutes.
items.answer: Energy consumed = power × time, so E = P × t = 1200 W × 20 × 60 s = 1200 × 1200 W s = 1.44 × 10⁶ J.

items.stem: An electric bulb is marked 60 W. What does this mean? How much energy does it consume if used for 1 hour?
items.answer: A bulb marked 60 W means that it consumes 60 J of electrical energy in one second. Energy consumed in one hour E = P × t = 60 W × 1 h = 60 Wh = 0.06 kWh.

items.stem: The rating of an electric heater is 1100 W, 220 V. Calculate its resistance when it operates at 220 V. Also calculate the energy consumed in kWh in the month of November if the heater is used daily for four hours at the rated voltage.
items.answer: From P = V²/R, R = V²/P = (220 V × 220 V)/1100 W = 44 Ω. November has 30 days, so the total time of use is 4 h × 30 = 120 h. Energy consumed E = P × t = 1100 W × 120 h = 132000 Wh = 132 kWh.

items.stem: (a) Electric fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. Why? (b) An electric oven of rating 2 kW, 220 V is operated in a domestic circuit with a current rating of 5 A. What result would you expect? Explain.
items.answer: (a) An electric fuse is a safety device which melts and breaks the circuit when too large a current flows, and so prevents damage to appliances and electrical fires; that is why it is an important component of a domestic circuit. (b) The current drawn is I = P/V = 2000 W/220 V = 9.09 A. Since the current drawn by the oven is more than 5 A, the fuse wire will melt and the supply will be cut off.

items.stem: An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 840 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 360 W when the heating is at the minimum. The voltage is 220 V. What are the current and the resistance in each case?
items.answer: From P = VI, I = P/V. (a) When heating is at the maximum rate: I = 840 W/220 V = 3.82 A and R = V/I = 220/3.82 = 57.6 Ω. (b) When heating is at the minimum rate: I = 360 W/220 V = 1.64 A and R = V/I = 220 V/1.64 A = 134.15 Ω.

items.stem: Express the electrical energy (1 kWh) in joules.
items.answer: 1 kWh = 1000 watts × 60 min = 1000 × 60 × 60 watt-seconds = 3.6 × 10⁶ watt-seconds = 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.
items.ocr: The printed stem reads 'Express the electrical energy in Joules'; '(1 kWh)' is added from the worked solution, which converts 1 kWh.

items.stem: (a) What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits? (b) An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic electric circuit (220 V) that has a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? Explain.
items.answer: (a) To avoid overloading: (i) too many high power rating appliances (electric iron, geyser, A.C.) should not be switched on at the same time, and (ii) too many electrical appliances should not be operated from a single socket. (b) P = 2 kW = 2000 W and V = 220 volt, so I = P/V = 2000/220 = 9 A. The current drawn by the oven is more than 5 A, so the fuse will melt and the power supply in this circuit would be cut off.

items.stem: In a household electric circuit different appliances are connected in parallel to one another. Give two advantages of such connections. Two bulbs rated 100 W, 200 V and 25 W, 200 V are connected in parallel to a 200 V supply. What will be the current drawn from the supply line?
items.answer: (a) Each appliance gets the full supply voltage and can draw the current it requires. (b) Each appliance can be switched on and off, and so controlled, individually. For the bulbs, R₁ = V²/P₁ = (200 × 200)/100 = 400 Ω and R₂ = V²/P₂ = (200 × 200)/25 = 1600 Ω. Their parallel resistance R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = (1600 × 400)/2000 = 320 Ω, so the current drawn I = V/R = 200/320 = 0.63 A.

items.stem: A torch bulb is rated 5.0 V and 500 mA. Calculate (i) its power, (ii) its resistance and (iii) the energy consumed when it is lighted for four hours.
items.answer: Given V = 5.0 volt and I = 500 mA = 500/1000 = 0.5 A. (i) Power P = I × V = 0.5 × 5 = 2.5 W. (ii) Resistance R = V/I = 5/0.5 = 10 Ω. (iii) Energy E = power × time = (2.5/1000) kW × 4 h = 0.01 kWh.

items.stem: What is electric power?
items.answer: The rate at which electrical energy is consumed, or converted into heat, is known as electric power. P = W/t = I²Rt/t = I²R, and also P = I × V, i.e. power = current × potential difference. Its SI unit is the watt.

items.stem: If 0.18 ampere of current is drawn by an electric bulb when it is connected to a source of 220 volts, find the power of the bulb.
items.answer: Given current I = 0.18 ampere and potential difference V = 220 volts. Power P = V × I = 220 × 0.18 = 39.6 W ≈ 40 watt (approximately).

items.stem: What is the commercial unit of electrical energy?
items.answer: Since the watt is a very small unit of power, the unit used in practice is the kilowatt, where 1 kilowatt = 1000 watts. As electrical energy = power × time, the commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called one unit, and 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

items.stem: An electric motor operates on a 50 V supply and draws a current of 13 A. If the motor yields a mechanical power of 130 W, what is the percentage efficiency of the motor?
items.answer: Current I = 13 A and input power P = V × I = 50 × 13 = 650 watt. Output power = 130 W. Efficiency = (output power/input power) × 100 = (130/650) × 100 = 20%.

items.stem: Two identical resistors, each of resistance 50 Ω, are connected (i) in series and (ii) in parallel, in turn, to a battery of 10 V. Calculate the ratio of power consumed in the combination of resistors in the two cases.
items.answer: (i) In series, Rs = R₁ + R₂ = 50 Ω + 50 Ω = 100 Ω, so Ps = V²/Rs = 10²/100 = 1 W. (ii) In parallel, Rp = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = (50 × 50)/100 = 25 Ω, so Pp = V²/Rp = 10²/25 = 4 W. Required ratio Ps : Pp = 1 W : 4 W = 1 : 4.
items.ocr: The parallel line printed as 'Pp = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂)'; it is the resistance Rp = 25 Ω, as the next line uses.

items.stem: A wire of resistance 20 ohm is bent in the form of a closed circle. What is the effective resistance between the two points at the ends of any diameter of the circle?
items.answer: A diameter divides the circle into two semicircles, each of resistance 20/2 = 10 ohms, and the two semicircles are connected in parallel between the ends of the diameter. So 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/10 + 1/10 = 2/10 = 1/5, giving R = 5 ohms.

items.stem: Two resistors with resistances 10 Ω and 15 Ω are to be connected to an emf of 12 V so as to obtain (i) minimum current, (ii) maximum current. How will you connect the resistance in each case? Calculate the strength of the total current in the circuit in the two cases.
items.answer: (i) To obtain the minimum current the two resistors should be connected in series, so that Rs = 10 Ω + 15 Ω = 25 Ω and Imin = 12 V/25 Ω = 0.48 A. (ii) To obtain the maximum current the two resistors should be connected in parallel, so that Rp = (15 × 10)/(15 + 10) = 6 Ω and Imax = 12/6 = 2 A.
items.ocr: The printed parallel formula shows '15 Ω × 10 Ω / 15 Ω × 10 Ω' in the denominator; restored to (15 × 10)/(15 + 10) = 6 Ω, the value the solution then uses.
